likewise, the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which also directly perceives form, should also arise from seeds of its own kind. [Response: Visual consciousness itself is capable of perfuming its own aspects; thus, the aspect and the seeing arise from seeds of their own kind.
Eighth, it cannot permeate the views, as the characteristics [of the views] arise separately. Question: If that is so, the eye does not take the eight views as its object;
yet the eight views arise with distinct characteristics.
Since the six [consciousnesses] are already capable of being common [to all], [why is this distinction made]?

The eight views share the same category. Answer: The eighth view also shares the same single category. If that were so, there would be the fault of confusion among the various dharmas, just as the sixth consciousness, within a single moment, takes the eighteen realms as its objects.
Since the object (*ālambana*) and the seeing (*darśana*) arise from the same seed, there would be the fault of confusion among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, there would be the error of confusion among the three realms (*dhātu*). According to the second [position], the object is not produced; the object is merely pre-existing.
There are also two faults.
First is the fault of contradicting the teachings.
If the preceding evolving consciousnesses do not perfuse and form the seeds for that eighth fundamental consciousness, [the system fails].
The *Abhidharma-sūtra* states: "All phenomena reside within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the consciousness likewise resides within phenomena;
they serve as mutual causes for one another."
Furthermore, it would constantly possess the nature of being an effect; secondly, there would be the fault of confusion among the realms (*dhātu*).
Moreover, if the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) were of the same seed-type, it would be like arising in a lower stage with the divine eye of a higher stage.

Since it is already granted that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) takes those two faculties as its objective part (nimittabhāga), it follows that the fundamental consciousness of the desire realm and those two faculties arise from the same seed.

This entails the error that the eye-faculty of a higher realm and the consciousness of a lower realm would likewise arise from the same seed. If one were to argue that the eighth consciousness and its objective part have different seeds because the former cannot be perfumed (vāsita), [that argument is untenable].
First, the previous statement is not precise;
second, there is the fault of contradicting reason.
[Question: How can the eight co-existent characteristics (*sahabhū-lakṣaṇa*) be different from one another? The second master says:
If one holds that the perception of a form arises from a distinct seed, there are likewise three faults:
first, the fallacy that a conventional phenomenon would arise from a seed;
for example, when taking atoms as its object, those atoms lack intrinsic substance.
However, it is merely a conceptual construction that analyzes [matter] down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun) states below: "It does not mean that the ultimate atom possesses a real intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 54, says:
The establishment of atoms is not due to their having substantial existence;
therefore, atoms are neither produced nor extinguished.
If these characteristics are differentiated and perfumed into seeds, they subsequently give rise to manifest activity.

If atoms possessed substantiality and also underwent arising and ceasing, then the fault of their being inconsistent with conditions would likewise apply; thus, these two [positions] contradict the sacred teachings.
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun*, fascicle 18, states:
This means that all atoms are established merely as conceptual constructs;
they lack substantial reality. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 54), it is not because they possess a substantial entity that [atoms] arise from distinct seeds;
rather, if they were to arise from distinct seeds, they would necessarily possess a substantial entity.
Thus, it contradicts the holy teachings that the three types of provisional phenomena can act as perfumers.
Since one establishes atoms through provisional conceptual wisdom,
and since it is admitted that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*)— being provisional— can perfume seeds.
This would contradict the second [position], as a provisional dharma cannot be non-causal. The third master says:
"The seeing and image aspects are, according to their respective cases, either identical or different in terms of their seeds."
It is like taking tortoise hair or rabbit horns as objects;
their characteristics and the seeing [of them] belong to the same category,
because they lack intrinsic nature and their objective parts are merely provisional.
There is no separate perfuming of seeds;
rather, it follows the power of perception to carry along the perfumed seeds,
just as when one takes the five sense-faculties as the substantial reality of conditioned phenomena.
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and their respective bases (*lakṣya*) arise from distinct seeds;

because the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) have determinate causes, they do not become confused with one another. However, regarding the marks and their bases, one school asserts that they arise from the same seed.
One view holds that they are of different seeds.

Although there are two aspects—the aspect of appearance (*nimitta*) and the substantial entity (*vastu*)—it is also reasonable for them to be of different seeds, because the seeds of immediate and remote conditions are distinct.
For example, when the eighth [consciousness] takes an aspect as its object, the aspect and the substantial entity are of the same seed.

If it is granted that a single type arises as both an aspect (*nimitta*) and a non-aspect (*anākāra*), then there would also be the simultaneous loss of the two [types of] body-faculties (*kāyendriya*).
Since the aspect and the substance (*dravya*) arise from the same seed, why do the two body-faculties not [arise simultaneously]?
Furthermore, when the six [consciousnesses] take their objects, if the aspectual portion (*nimittabhāga*) is merely provisional (*prajñapti*), [then...]
In this case, there arises a single fallacy of conflating the provisional with the real. This term "provisional" does not refer to things such as jars;
because it acts as a perfuming agent (*vāsana*), it is merely designated as "provisional" because it lacks the functional capacity of a sense organ (*indriya*) to produce consciousness.
Based on these characteristics, some say that the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the substance (dravya) are identical, while others say they are distinct;
however, one should apply diligent effort toward this point. Furthermore, it is explained that if the characteristic and the substance arise from the same kind (jāti), [then they are identical].

The sense organs such as the eye, which are transformed by the eighth consciousness, exist substantially as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) because they possess the functional activity of an organ.
If the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises, it is produced by the sixth consciousness;
although it arises from the same seed as its primary object (*ālambana*), [it is nonetheless distinct].
Because it arises conditioned by the sixth view and is comprised within conceptual transformation, it lacks practical utility.
Since it is not a mere designation lacking a basis, there is no fault of conflating the conventional and the real into a single category.

However, regarding the similarity or difference of seeds: there are cases where the nature of the seed is identical to that of the vision; or cases where the nature is identical while the connection and the seed differ; or cases where the nature of the objective part (nimitta-bhāga) is determined according to the substance (dravya) of the vision, such that its nature is indeterminate; or even when there is a substance.
The characteristics and perceptions are identical in their essence, whether arising or non-arising.
Because this is not fixed,
the Tripitaka Master [Xuanzang] used one verse to clarify these distinctions, saying:
The objective realm does not follow the mind;
the solitary reflection arises solely from the aspect;
that which carries a substantial essence pertains to both the mental object and its basis.
The nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) and so forth are explained according to their respective applications as stated in the *Śūyāo* (Essential Summary).

Because the meaning is somewhat difficult, it is further elaborated here. First, the nature and object of the sphere are established, and subsequently, the non-conformity [to mental construction] is revealed. What is meant by "nature-sphere" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*)?

That which arises from actual seeds and possesses substantial reality and function is called an "objective realm" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) when the cognizing mind apprehends its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For example, the five sensory objects transformed by the eighth consciousness when the body resides in the desire realm.
That which arises from actual seeds and is further transformed by causes and conditions is called the "objective sphere" (*viṣaya*). This refers to the five consciousnesses,
such as the visual consciousness, along with the sixth consciousness that arises simultaneously with them.
When direct perception (pratyakṣa) takes an object as its condition, it apprehends the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of that object;
this very image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is also a "real object" (svabhāva-viṣaya),
because the image conforms to its substance (pratibimba-anusāra).
Other dharmas may be understood by analogy. Thus, there are four ways in which the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) does not conform to its subject:
first, it does not necessarily share the same moral nature—whether wholesome or defiled—as its perceiving subject;
second, it does not necessarily belong to the same realm of existence (dhātu-bandhana) as its perceiving subject.
Third, it does not arise as being of the same type as its corresponding cognitive faculty (*ālambaka*).

Fourth, it does not correspond to its cognitive faculty in terms of being a maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth. Within this, although there may be cases where the object shares the same realm (*dhātu*) and the same category (*nikāya*) as the corresponding mind, such is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object itself.
It is not by virtue of the power of the cognizing mind that this nature, realm, stage, and so forth are established;
thus they are called "objective objects" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) that do not follow the mind.
For example, the five consciousnesses can be associated with all three moral natures.
Both their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their substance (*dravya*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
They do not arise from the five [consciousnesses], yet they also pertain to all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
The remainder should be understood by analogy.
Although the five groups of consciousness are of an indeterminate nature,
even though their nature remains the same when taking the five sensory objects as their conditions,
the aspect-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) each maintain their own respective natures.
It is not because it follows that objectifying mind (*ālambana-citta*) that it becomes indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
the rest should be understood accordingly. If the solitary, distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the five objects (*viṣaya*) of its own realm as its object, and so forth.
However, that object abides in its own nature rather than attaining a self-nature;
yet, natures, seeds, and so forth are likewise subject to the five conditions.
This explains the second phrase.
This means that the cognizing mind merely transforms into an appearance;
there is no separate second entity as an underlying essence.
Even if such an essence were to exist, [it would not be perceived].
However, those image-aspects (nimitta-bhāga) do not produce the fundamental reality (svabhāva),
because that fundamental reality consists of dharmas that are unarisen and so forth.
These image-aspects...
Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness takes as its object the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) manifested by the five mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness,
it is called "solely from the seeing-part" (*dṛṣṭimātra*) because it arises from the same seed as its subjective perceiver.

For example, when solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes such things as empty flowers or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as its objects, these all arise of the same nature as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).

Alternatively, taking unconditioned phenomena as an object constitutes the third case, or the fourth; [likewise] when it takes the five mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness as its objects.
Alternatively, there is the fourth alternative: those that take empty flowers and the like as their objects. These images have four [characteristics] derived from the seeing [aspect]:
first, they are of the same nature as the seeing aspect, being either wholesome or defiled;
second, they belong to the same realm.
Third, they are identical in being of one kind;
fourth, they are identical in being both matured (*vipāka*) and non-matured,
because they do not arise as substantial entities but are merely transformations of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is of the same nature as this realm because it is the object of the perceiving mind; thus,
the objective aspect is subsumed within the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga).

The name "solitary shadow" (pratibimba) refers exclusively to the aspect of the seeing [faculty]. Question: Regarding the appearance of a flower in the sky, is it classified as matter (rūpa) or as mind (citta)?
If it is matter, how can it share the same nature [as the consciousness]?
If it is mind, its original intention is to take matter as its object.
How does the mind transform its objective aspect (nimittabhāga) to serve as an object? Answer:
That which is falsely conceptualized is the color-form of pervasive imagination (parikalpita-rūpa); that which is merely vaguely perceived is [the dependent nature].
Although it is not itself a parikalpita (imagined nature), because it belongs to that same category, it is also subsumed under it;
for since it is of the same seed, it shares the same nature of consciousness. Furthermore, the term "parikalpa" has the meaning of "discrimination."
It is not merely a matter of grasping with the mind.

Otherwise, there would be the fault of failing to encompass all phenomena, as in the case of a feverish illness impairing the eyes and so forth; thus, seeing yellow when it is not yellow is not [a function of] the sixth consciousness.
Seeing yellow when it is not yellow belongs to the sixth consciousness.
This is because visual consciousness does not apprehend its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Although this is not a mind that clings to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
it may still be termed "form arising from pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpita-rūpa*).

However, the seeds that are perfumed are subsumed under their respective primary natures (*svabhāva*). Question: For example, when subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes as its objects the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as the appearances of empty flowers, rabbit horns, and so forth, which are the objects of ordinary beings—[how are these seeds categorized]?
Question: By which category is this dharma subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed under the *dharmasabhāga* (homogeneity of dharmas).

This is because its nature is provisional (*prajñapti*), and the *dharmasabhāga* is a broader category that encompasses all objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*) conditioned by unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is because they differ from contaminated phenomena in that they are not based on false objects; alternatively, even those that take empty flowers and the like as their objects are included within the form produced by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), for the term "pervasive conceptualization" refers to discursive discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the second point, "interpreting as one wishes": Question: When the body is in a higher realm and one perceives the forms of the desire realm with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), under which category is the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of these forms subsumed?
Answer: One school says: [it is subsumed under the category of the same realm].
Although it is not a solitary-image [object], it is nevertheless seen by that [consciousness],
because the specific form of that meditative absorption does not arise in a lower stage due to the difference in its level of attachment (*bhūmi-bandhana*).

This [seeing] arises from being bound to the same realm (*dhātu*) but not from being of the same type (*jāti*). If that is so, how can it take its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object? Answer: That which directly grasps the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the objective reality (*vastu*) is called "attaining its own nature. If that is so, then since subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth as its objects, seeing should be distinct [from it]. Answer: Although it attains its own nature, [it does not constitute a separate seeing].
Because it is fundamentally non-arising; secondly,
it is said that the objective realm does not follow the mind,
because it takes as its substantial basis the color-form transformed by the eighth consciousness itself.
Because it constitutes a distinct category;
because its nature is inherently indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and does not depend on the mind;
and because, although it is a fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*), it actually belongs to a higher realm yet resembles that of a lower realm.
Because the function of the supernormal power of the divine eye is superior, that which is attained above resembles that which is below.

This is not the same as taking the higher [levels] as an object; rather, one must first induce the fruit of the supernormal power and the fruit of meditative concentration, and only when they become similar to those [lower levels] can they be taken as objects. Furthermore, it is explained that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) that arises is the fruit of karma.
Although the divine eye of the supernormal power of the divine eye arises from visual consciousness, it is not matter that is the fruit of supernormal power;
because it takes as its object the matter that is the karmic fruit of the desire realm,
that which is transformed and produced by the mind that is the fruit of supernormal power is what serves as the object for that consciousness.

Just as the eye-consciousness arising from the eye that is the fruit of karma carries the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of matter that is the fruit of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), what prevents the mind that is the fruit of meditative absorption from carrying matter that is the fruit of karma?

Of the two previous explanations, the former is superior; the latter is difficult to resolve and should be further considered. Question: Just as there are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena that mutually take one another as objects...
And what do the non-associated [factors] and the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) subsume? Answer: There are two interpretations.
First, they are the same as the dharmas of the homogeneous class (sabhāgatā).
Second, they are the matter of pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita-rūpa).

The previous explanation is correct. Question: Since the pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*) is established within form (*rūpa*), why is it not [so] established within the mind (*citta*) and other [factors]?
Answer: An aggregate of form is not an object of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*);
the pervasive imagination is established in the same manner as that [aggregate].
Mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) can only take objects;
since pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) does not take an object, it is not established [as such].
It may be admitted that dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) are so established.
The statement that there are twenty-four [mental factors] is established according to their predominance,
just as the various mental concomitants are established according to their predominance;
furthermore, it is established according to what is appropriate in each case.
It also belongs to that cognizing mind. Question: Do the distracted eyes and ears of a higher stage take a lower stage as their object?
If they do not take a lower stage as their object, how is it that those in a higher stage can see what is below?
If it takes the lower-level *nimitta-bhāga* as its object, how is it categorized?
Answer: A distracted mind does not take the lower level as its object because it is too distant.
It is said that seeing what is above while taking what is below as the object is based on the universal resultants (*viśeṣa-phala*).

Furthermore, when the visual and auditory consciousnesses are analyzed separately, they can also take what is below as their object, such as when one perceives the arising of the three calamities in lower realms and conceives various perceptions. Regarding the staff, there are two interpretations—taking it as either oneself or another—which are not fixed.
The fetters are subsumed under the higher realms from the perspective of their aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*),
because outflowing (*sāsrava*) [dharmas] do not increase in accordance with a different realm. Some say they are bound to the lower realms,
because by relying on the signs (*nimitta*) of the lower realms, they are perfumed (*vāsita*) and thus formed as lower.
Because they are not of the nature of outflows (*āsrava*), [the outflows] do not increase therein;
however, this is difficult to conceive.
This explains the third phrase.
This means that when the cognizing mind takes an object as its focal point,
it relies upon a supporting substance and does not attain an intrinsic nature;
thus, this aspect of the image (nimitta-bhāga) is determined to be indeterminate in nature.
The seeds are also not fixed, whether they are derived from the cognizing mind or from the perceived object.
Some are of the same substance,
some are of the same appearance,
and others are of different substances.
The name "with-substratum" (sābhilāpa) applies to both the mental state and its object-base;
it is like the seventh consciousness taking the eighth as its object.
This is a case of subsuming the characteristics under the aspect, and it is of a nature that is obscured (nivṛta).
Regarding the nature of being non-obscured: Question—The shadow arises based upon the substance;
because it originates from the primary [substance], it is termed "non-obscured.
The shadow is produced in dependence upon the substance.
It is called "maturation" (vipāka) by way of its substantial nature.
Answer: It is undefiled (anivṛta) by its essential category;
both the reflection and the original are undefiled.
Retribution (vipāka) is based on the requital of karma;
the image is not retribution. Question: Retribution is based on the projection by karma;
the image is not retribution.
The unobscured is the substance of retribution;
the image is not unobscured. Answer: The category of nature is broad;
both the original and the image are unobscured.
The nature of maturation is restricted;

it applies only to the primary [object] and does not extend to the reflected image. Question: When the five consciousnesses take the five objects as their conditions, why are they not both judged to be identical in aspect?
The seventh [category] is the staff; the eighth is birth.
Regarding the distinction between the two natures of characteristics: the answer is that the objects of the five conditions are merely objective in nature;
they are exclusively *svabhāva-viṣaya* (objective realms) and do not follow the mind.
Regarding the objects of the seven [consciousnesses] that take conditions as their objects:

since these objects encompass both those that are mental and those that are non-mental, they are categorized according to both meanings. Question: Why do the five [sensory consciousnesses] take only form as their object?
These are exclusively *svabhāva-viṣaya* (objective realms).
As for the realms, they are not divided into two;
they function interchangeably and universally perceive all six objects.

The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) should be understood as pervading both the sentient and the insentient. Answer: Although they are called "objective aspects" because they serve as conditions for mutual cognition, since these aspects pertain to multiple phenomena, they function accordingly.
When not yet engaged in mutual cognition, they simply take their own respective objects as conditions.
Therefore, it is said that the five [consciousnesses] take their own nature as their object.
If the independent manovijñāna takes an object, its scope is broad and pervasive, and it also falls under the fourth category.
Some say that the "object with substance" (dai-zhi) is included within both the "sentient" (qing) and the "original" (ben).

If the manifest aspect (nimitta) is separated from its substance (dravya) and separated from the seeing [aspect], it is then subsumed under the category of the homogeneous (sabhāga). Question: If that were so, the homogeneous would necessarily be substantially existent (dravyasat). Answer: Even if one calculates it thus, there is no fault.

Just as the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is merely seeds and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it does not preclude the seventh [link] from also being included within "name" (*nāman*). Alternatively, it is explained that this is not so;
the seventh link is included in "name-and-form" based on its manifestation, but it is not a [constituent] link (*aṅga*) in itself.
The *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is dissociated [from mind];
it is merely conventional and does not extend to the real.
If one were to hold that present phenomena cannot be objects of cognition, [it would follow that they do not exist].
The *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) of dharmas that are neither mind nor matter cannot take any of the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object;
the seeds and so forth should likewise be considered the *sabhāgatā* of dharmas.
Since that [other case] is not so, how could this be otherwise?
Therefore, it cannot be said that there is a definitive judgment apart from seeing,
because it must necessarily follow one or the other.
The interpretation that it belongs to the non-dharmic homogeneous class (*adharmasabhāga*) is correct. Therefore,
it is determined that the seventh [type], the detached view, is subsumed under the homogeneous class of both the substantial entity and the phenomenon (*dravya-dharma-sabhāga*).
This is not the correct explanation; I shall now provide a supplementary interpretation.

Regarding the statement that "that which possesses a substantial object (saviṣaya) penetrates both the mental state and its basis," it is as in the case where uncontaminated (anāsrava) states take one another as their mutual objects.
Just as the seventh [consciousness] takes the eighth as its object,
the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the untainted (anāsrava) is virtuous when derived from the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga), but is indeterminate (avyākṛta) when derived from the substance (dravya).
The rest should be understood accordingly.
Therefore it is said: "The aspect that carries the substance (dai-zhi) penetrates both the phenomenal aspect (qing-ben) and the seeing-part (jian-fen).
Furthermore, even if a substance exists, its relationship with the seeing-part may be either fixed or indeterminate.
Regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned, and the outflowing and the non-outflowing:
reflect upon these according to their meaning.
If one follows the original commentary:
When the outflowing and non-outflowing [dharmas] and so forth serve as mutual objects of cognition,
this corresponds to the fourth alternative.
Regarding "nature-seeds" and so forth, they should be applied accordingly.
This provides a general explanation of the first three phrases.
That is to say, within these first three phrases,
the determination of their nature, seeds, and so forth, according to what is appropriate, cannot be treated by a single uniform rule.
There are cases where the nature (dhātu) follows the mind but the seed (bīja) does not;
there are cases where the nature follows the mind but the seed does not;
and there are cases where the realm (dhātu) and the seed follow the nature of the mind but do not [necessarily] follow it.
There are cases where both follow together,
and there are cases where neither follows together.
For instance, when the eighth [consciousness] takes the divine eye or ear as its object.

The nature [of the eighth consciousness] conforms to the seeds, but it does not conform to the realm. Question: Regarding the five and six [consciousnesses], when they take the five sensory objects as their conditions and apprehend their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), their nature does not conform to the mind.
How is it that the nature of the eighth [consciousness] conforms to the mind? Answer: The eighth is fundamental; the others are derivative.
Furthermore, the substance of the five and six consciousnesses permeates all three natures,
whereas the eight consciousnesses in the causal stage are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Thus, the eighth consciousness is conditioned by the seventh.
The nature is both identical and non-identical,
because it penetrates both the phenomenal and the fundamental.
The realm is identical while the seeds are non-identical.

Such categories as these may be fully understood through reflection. Furthermore, regarding the seven conditions and eight causes, they follow one another in substance and are non-obscured (*anivṛta*).
They cannot arise from all eight [conditions], for they are maturation (*vipāka*).
Therefore, it is said that they "correspond accordingly. Moreover, a fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be applied.
There are objects that exist as real entities which do not conform to the mind and are "solitary images" arising solely from the aspect of perception (*darśana-bhāga*).
This refers to the sixth, distracted mental consciousness when it shares the same object as the five sensory consciousnesses,
and at that very moment, takes such things as a rabbit's horn as its object.
As well as the eighth consciousness, the sovereign mind (citta-rāja):
their objective spheres are not dependent on the mind;
mental factors (caitta) possess only projected images, which follow solely from the aspect (darśana-bhāga).

The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is provisional because it has no distinct seed; therefore: Question: Just as the sixth consciousness, when taking the eighth consciousness as its object, perceives its objective aspect but does not perceive its seeing aspect (darśana-bhāga), are the objective aspects carried by these two [the sixth and the seventh] the same or different?
Answer: They arise from the same seed as the perceiving mind. Question: Regarding the objective aspect that takes that seeing aspect as its object...
It is thus granted that [the image] is of the same seed as the six types of views.

How is it that this object and its image are of the same seed? Answer: Because the image-part (nimittabhāga) is conventionally derived from the perceiving subject (ālambaka), it is of the same seed as the view.

Regarding the nature of objects: those that do not follow the mind (*asārūpya*) also possess a substantial basis (*sanimitta*), and they penetrate both the subjective state (*sākāra*) and the objective essence (*sanimitta*).
This refers to the case where the distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) shares the same object as the five [sensory] consciousnesses;

at that very moment, it also takes the eighth [consciousness] and so forth as its object. There are objective entities (*vastu*) that do not follow the mind, as well as "solitary images" (*pratibimba*) that arise solely from the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), the pervasive [part], and the fundamental [nature].
This refers to the case where the distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) simultaneously takes the eighteen realms as its object;
when compared to the five sensory consciousnesses which take the five objects as their common objects,
this is termed a "real object" (*svabhāvaviṣaya*) that does not follow the mind.
The seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) are associated with both the affective and the fundamental [fetters].

In contrast, when viewed in relation to the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*), they pertain exclusively to the view-fetters. Question: Regarding the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that takes suchness as its object, under which category is it subsumed? Answer: It may be subsumed under either the affective or the fundamental [fetters].
From the perspective of its substance, it is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
from the perspective of its aspect, it is called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This is because it is admitted that the unconditioned is a provisional designation based upon consciousness.
Alternatively, it may be categorized according to its nature, its object, or its associated mind;
the same principle may be applied to the *sāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya*. If distinguished according to their seeds (*bīja*), [the classification is as follows].

That is to say, it follows from the [first] view alone, or else from the fourth alternative: when non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) takes true suchness (tathatā) as its object, the objective realm (svabhāva-viṣaya) does not conform [to the subject].
The substance is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) that is virtuous, while the wisdom is the conditioned (saṃskṛta) that is virtuous.
Seeing is established as a distinct seed;
it cannot be perfumed by signs.

Because it apprehends its own objective sphere (*svaviṣaya*), it is said not to follow the mind. Question: Regarding the visual consciousness and other sensory consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, which rely upon the superior faculties of that stage and take the forms and signs (*rūpa-nimitta*) of that same stage as their objects—what is their objective part (*nimittabhāga*)? Answer: There are two interpretations.

As previously stated, when consciousness of a higher stage takes a lower stage as its object, one [school] claims it is "bound" to that higher stage because it takes the matter (rūpa) of that lower stage as its object;

therefore, there should be "increase" (anuśaya). However, this is not an increase, because it does not possess the nature of an outflow (āsrava). If one asks how defilement arises [in this case]: if one has been born in a higher stage, one has already abandoned the defilements of the lower stage.
If one in a lower stage takes the superior form and so forth as an object, the supernormal powers of the eye and ear also suppress defilements.

How then could the innate [defilements] not be suppressed? Even if they were not suppressed, they would arise because of the falling away from meditative concentration. One opinion states that they are bound to the lower stage in accordance with the mind.
Since the perfuming mind belongs to a lower stage, how could it take a higher stage as its object and transform it into a lower-phase *nimitta-bhāga*?

Furthermore, one would not be able to apprehend its own nature (*svabhāva*). [If it were argued that] through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), it spontaneously takes the higher stage as its object and thus apprehends its own nature—both of these positions are difficult to maintain.

Commentary: Question: Since [the consciousness] is situated in a lower realm, how can it take a higher realm as its object? Answer: Because the afflictions are induced by the power of another’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Question: What is the manner in which a Brahmā descends? Commentary says:
The coarse matter of the lower realms does not serve as a basis for the higher realms;
rather, [beings] transform themselves into the bodies of the higher realms and rely upon them.

Thus, the environment (*bhājana*) of the higher realm relies upon the environment of the lower realm as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Question: Since they have come to the lower realm, do they not take the lower realm as an object of perception?

Just as when Aśvajit ascends, it is permitted that [the mind] takes the upper realm as its object; the answer is that it also takes the lower realm as its object. Question: If this is so, under what category is the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed within the upper realm.

Because there is no matter resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-rūpa*) in the desire realm, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is subsumed under the desire realm itself, as it does possess matter resulting from supernormal powers.
Question: Does that which belongs to a lower realm take as its object the bodies and environments (*deha-bhājana*) of those higher realms?
By which category is this phrase subsumed? Answer: It is the "objective realm that does not follow the mind.
This is because the determinate, supernormal, and fruition-produced matter (niyata-viṣaya, abhijñā-phala, and vipākaja-rūpa) induced by that [mind] serve as the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga);
thus, their underlying essence, realm, and seeds all do not follow the mind. Question: This may be so for the eighth [consciousness].

Since it is already admitted that the eye and other faculties can also take higher levels as their objects, would it not follow that those associated with a higher level are tainted (sāsrava) by the increase of afflictions belonging to a different realm? Answer: This is because the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is not, by its own nature, a defilement (*āsrava*).
Alternatively, it may be that due to the power of karma, [the faculties] do not increase across different realms;

however, those induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) increase one another without mutual obstruction. Another interpretation holds that it is simply because the eighth consciousness, induced from above, produces the visual faculty and so forth through the power of supernormal transformation (*nirmāṇa*);
thus, the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) arising therefrom are themselves the fruits of karma.
There is no fault of non-increase (anuvṛddhi) for those belonging to the lower realms,
just as when supernormal powers transform things into fish, rice, and so forth;
the matter resulting from the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-rūpa*) induced by the sixth consciousness serves as the substantial basis (*upādāna*) for the eighth [consciousness].
Alternatively, although one may take another's eight [bases] as a pledge,
the matter-form that is the fruit of karma belongs to the desire realm.
The fourth fascicle states that the three— odor, flavor, and tangibility— constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Because it is bound exclusively to the desire realm,
the two interpretations are left to one's discretion;
yet even from the perspective of logical principle, this is difficult to maintain.

This should be investigated: When the eighth [consciousness] of the lower realm takes the meditative absorption (samāpatti) as its object, what is the nature of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective image) of the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously?
Answer: It corresponds to the karmic fruit of the activity of the mental factors that take it as their objective support.
They are of the same kind and bound to the same lower realm, as they do not possess distinct substantial entities.

Question: When the solitary, distracted mind takes a past object as its condition, what is the nature of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five sense organs? Answer: It is according to what is appropriate for each case.
This is explained according to the previous principle.
Regarding the explanation that "solitary images arise solely from the *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual portion)," Ximing states:
All objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga), such as atoms (paramāṇu) and flowers in the sky (taimira-puṣpa), are perfumed to form seeds.
Question: Since these arise from seeds, why are atoms and the like said to be merely conventional (prajñapti)?
The commentary explains:
It is called "provisional" because its substance does not arise;
it is established as "real" based on the existence of seeds and the manifestation of their characteristics. Now, an objection is raised:
If it is claimed that the unarisen nature is itself the provisional,
then the ripening mind, mental factors, and so forth should be provisional rather than real,
because each of them is individually incapable of perfuming seeds.
If it is argued that because those [objects] still involve conceptualization and deliberation (*ālambana*), they are real and not provisional,
then it would follow that the distinction between the provisional and the real is not established by whether seeds produce substantial entities or do not produce them.
Furthermore, the five sensory consciousnesses, as resultant minds (*vipāka-citta*), take the five objects as their objective aspects (*nimitta*).
First, it is not an object of cognitive apprehension;
second, because it cannot be perfumed, it must be considered provisional rather than real.
Since this [the ālayavijñāna] is not provisional, how could that [the *paratantra-svabhāva*] be so?

If that which possesses the function of being non-obstructive due to its unique characteristic of being partless is designated as "provisional," then the form produced at will within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)—
which the treatises describe as unobstructed— should likewise be considered provisional rather than real.
If you grant this, then the gold,
silver, milk, and so forth transformed by the sovereign power of those in the eighth stage and above would not be substantially existent.
Furthermore, it is just as in the case of form and other [sensory objects].
Whether as substance or as characteristic, they may be either provisional or real, yet they are subsumed within the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*).
If so, how are the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) subsumed?
If they were subsumed within the unconditioned, they would currently possess arising and ceasing.
If it is argued that since material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are currently conditioned by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how can they be called "matter" (*rūpa*)?
If it is argued that the same difficulty applies to mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), and if it is further argued that they are [matter] because they share the same generic character (*sabhāgatā*).
How could there be a homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) that arises from seeds?
Furthermore, if atoms were to arise from seeds perfumed individually, there would be five faults;
three of these faults are as previously stated in the position that [atoms] arise solely from distinct seeds.
The fourth is the fault of improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
The fifty-fourth [sūtra] states:
"It is known through five signs."
This is called "improper mental attention regarding atoms.
That is to say, [the notion] that within a collection of matter there exist various atoms abiding by way of their own intrinsic nature should be known as the first type of improper mental attention.
Once it has arisen from its seed, it abides as its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Fifth is the fault of contradicting correct reasoning (*yukti*).
The treatise states: "By means of conceptual wisdom (*parikalpita-prajñā*), regarding the coarse characteristics of form..."
By gradually breaking down and reducing [matter] until it can no longer be reduced,
one conventionally designates it as an "ultimate atom" (paramāṇu); yet,
fundamentally, there is no substantial entity of an atom.
One merely establishes "extreme atoms" (paramāṇu) through conceptual construction;
thus, seeds are perfumed such that there exists the form of extreme atoms.
Just as there is truly no self, yet one falsely imagines it to be omnipresent throughout space.

To claim that seeds are produced through mutual perfuming, giving rise to a characteristic that pervades space and termed a "pervasive self," contradicts the scriptures which do not admit the existence of such a pervasive self.
It is not permitted to contradict reason.
Since both are mental conceptualizations, why would they not constitute seeds? The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) further states:
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are each distinct in their nature.
It is certainly not the case that consciousness does not arise from two conditions;
for it takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object, appearing as a semblance of the unconditioned.
Among the one hundred dharmas, it is subsumed under the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
It takes other realms as its object and is untainted (anāsrava) as its object.
Although it is not bound by different stages (bhūmi), it is not separated from form (rūpa) and the other aggregates.
Since all non-existent phenomena (dharma) must necessarily be inseparable from form and so forth as that which is absent,
they cannot possibly be of the same substance as the visual consciousness.

Regarding the statement, "Objects depend on internal consciousness; they are merely conventional. Consciousness is the basis for objects;
it is also ultimate," there are four interpretations.
The first says:
There is the duality of existence and non-existence;
it is a pervasive conceptual construction and a false fabrication,
existing only as conventional reality.
Dependence on another is dependent origination;
the objective sphere and its support are also the ultimate truth.
These two aspects are confronted as subject and object.
The image-aspect (nimittabhāga) is provisional and arises dependent upon the seeing-aspect;
as a provisional object, it exists only conventionally in dependence upon consciousness.
The seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) is real and is that which gives rise to the image-aspect.
These are conventional objects that exist in terms of ultimate reality.
Third, regarding the correspondence between superior and inferior:
worldly conventionality exists only as conventional reality.
The latter three forms also exist as ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sat*) prior [to their manifestation].
Regarding the fourth, which is distinguished by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*):
for ordinary beings, its object is exclusively conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
The "holy object" (*āryaviṣaya*) is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Although there are four interpretations, the meaning of the text here relies solely on the first pair. Question: Based on the objects perceived by ordinary beings and noble ones?
The parikalpita (imagined nature) should also be called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Answer: Even if this is granted, there is no fault.
As it says in the eighth [chapter] below:
"It may also be said to be the object of the wisdom of both ordinary beings and sages."
Since it is a condition for the noble ones, it is also called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
However, it is not called "existent" now,
because it is subsumed under the truth of non-existence (*abhāva-satya*).
